lead_insight.claim: System resilience requires adapting the whole technical and social system, because fixing one root cause only moves problems elsewhere.
lead_insight.context: A migration exposed interacting infrastructure and human workflow failures.
lead_insight.evidence: Systems resilient requires systemic adoption, and any sort of trying to like solve one particular insight, or one particular problem, we'll solve that one. The system is a healthy, growing organism that involves technical people, social things, like all of these coming together, and that's what Villas really needed.
lead_insight.speaker: instructor

insights.claim: Make changes easy to process, not merely easy to execute, because people need time, backpressure, and circuit breakers.
insights.context: Production changes became safer after adding friction through pull requests and explicit service lists.
insights.evidence: But making change easy is not the same thing as, you know, like making change easy to handle, it's not the same thing, it's making change easy to do. You want to make change easily handle but if it may change easy to do, what you're going to do is you're going to end up in a situation in which you're not insuring that you can think about a reason through that change.
insights.speaker: instructor

insights.claim: Adding workers and database connections can worsen PostgreSQL performance by increasing contention and I/O.
insights.context: The migration exposed a feedback loop where slow queries caused more connections and further slowdown.
insights.evidence: You can say, oh hey, think you're really slow, add more workers, which adds contention to Postgres, connections to Postgres, and slows it down. Not using the open account settings, by the way, literally just having a massive amount of connections available in postgres, you can meet some queries up to 45 slower, which then means the postgres is going to do a lot more IO, because more things are open in flight, they're just not doing anything.
insights.speaker: instructor

insights.claim: Metrics do not explain a system without an understanding of what the measurements represent.
insights.context: The team had metrics and data but could not initially form a coherent system hypothesis.
insights.evidence: And we had, we had metrics, we had data, the only school that you're building to understand the system, and most systems are actually by definition not understandable, and know one thing, whichever obvious, you're wrong. agent_prompts.title: Build a Change Preview CLI
agent_prompts.what_it_does: Creates deterministic plans showing which services a configuration change would modify.
agent_prompts.prompt: Build a small command-line tool called change-preview in Python. Read a YAML file containing services, dependencies, and desired versions, then read a second YAML file describing requested changes. Output a deterministic plain-text plan sorted by service name. Show each affected service, old value, new value, and whether dependencies are also affected. Reject unknown services, malformed versions, and circular dependencies with clear errors. Keep the implementation local and dependency-light. Add fixtures covering no changes, one direct change, one dependency cascade, invalid input, and circular dependencies. Add unit tests. Run `python -m pytest -q` as the validation command. Expected output is a passing test suite and a documented sample plan whose ordering remains identical across repeated runs.

origin.evidence: And ultimately, and again, around building safety and approachability, uh, we get to a very predictable workflow, right? And the workflow is, you go edit a file, you go do a PR, you go see the result of the plan, and you go apply it, right?

agent_prompts.title: Build a Documentation Miner
agent_prompts.what_it_does: Indexes scattered technical notes and returns ranked answers with source locations.
agent_prompts.prompt: Build a local documentation miner in Python. Accept a directory containing Markdown, plain text, GitHub-export text, chat-export text, and IRC-log fixtures. Extract headings, timestamps when present, and source filenames. Build a simple local index without network access. Support a search command that returns the five highest-scoring matching passages, breaking ties by filename and line number. Add a command that reports documents with repeated terms but no headings. Create fixed fixtures containing overlapping operational advice across formats. Add tests for indexing, ranking, tie-breaking, missing timestamps, and empty queries. Run `python -m pytest -q` as the validation command. Expected output is a passing test suite and identical search results across three repeated invocations.
